title: Bus Routes
statement:
A city transit authority operates several bus routes. Route i serves exactly the stops listed in routes[i], and every bus circles its route forever, so a passenger may board it at any stop of the route and step off at any other stop of the same route. A stop id appears at most once inside a single route, but the same stop may be served by many routes.

A passenger is waiting at stop source and wants to reach stop target. Boarding a bus costs one ride, and switching between buses at a shared stop costs one more ride, because the passenger has to board the second bus. Return the smallest number of rides needed to arrive at stop target, or -1 when target cannot be reached from source at all. When source equals target the passenger is already there and the answer is 0.

For example, with routes = [[1, 2, 7], [3, 6, 7]], source = 1 and target = 6, the passenger takes the first bus from stop 1 to stop 7 and then the second bus from stop 7 to stop 6, which is 2 rides.

Constraints: `1 <= routes.length <= 200` and `1 <= routes[i].length <= 50` and `0 <= routes[i][j] <= 10000` and `0 <= source <= 10000` and `0 <= target <= 10000`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(routes: number[][], source: number, target: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: The places you can stand are stops, but the decisions you make are which bus to board; ask what a single ride can change.
Two stops are one ride apart when some route contains both, so build that graph and look for the shortest path from source to target.
Precompute for every stop the list of routes serving it, then run BFS over route indices and return the ride count of the first visited route that contains target.

editorial.approach: Brute force searches the stop graph directly: it keeps a frontier of stops, and for every stop on the frontier it rescans all routes and all stops of those routes to find which stops are one bus away. With n total stop entries that rescanning costs O(n) work per expanded stop, so O(n^2) overall. The optimal version changes the vertex of the search. It first builds a hash map from stop id to the list of route indices serving that stop, then runs BFS over route indices instead of stops. A route is enqueued the first time it is reached, and the ride count recorded when it is reached is its distance in the route graph.
editorial.why_optimal: The input must be read at least once, so every correct algorithm is Omega(n) for n total stop entries, and a shortest path of k rides means exactly k-1 bus changes, which BFS discovers by scanning each route exactly once. The hash map adds only O(n) space and turns every which-routes-serve-this-stop question into a constant time lookup, so O(n) is the best achievable here. At the stated size of at most 200 routes of at most 50 stops the naive version is still fast, but the map-based traversal is the one that survives a real transit network.
editorial.pitfalls: Forgetting the source == target case and answering 1, or handling it after the graph has been built. Counting transfers instead of boardings, so the first bus is never paid for. Marking stops visited but not routes, which makes the same route get expanded again and again. Forgetting that a bus may be left at any stop of its route, not only at the stop where it was boarded. Returning the distance of whichever route reaches target first instead of the minimum over the routes that contain target, and answering -1 only when no route ever reaches it.
